searches.note: The four shared searches settled the appellation of Châteauneuf-du-Pape (the union of 1923, the decree of 15 May 1936, Baron Le Roy's dates, whether the decree of 1936 named thirteen varieties) and the papal castle of 1317 to 1333. One search restricted to the Brunier family's own domains returned nothing. Two searches went to dates that could not be found (Jacques Perrin's birth) or to a claim no source carried (the reclusive grandson at Rayas). No WebFetch was tried. Fifteen searches of the share are left unspent.

method: The fragment was written with no web search at all, resting on the Codex's library and region records and on the writer's memory; this recheck searched every fact beyond the Codex, the strongest first: the founders and owners with their years, the appellation and its decree, the sites and soils, the making and its months, the label words and every beat of the story.

Every source the fragment listed (the Codex's own library, its California and Rhône region records, and two reference books, none opened) is replaced by pages a search returned, read: search; marked primary where the result came from the producer's own domain (beaucastel.com, familleperrin.com, tablascreek.com, vieux-telegraphe.fr, clos-des-papes.fr), the growers' body of the appellation (chateauneuf.com), Inter Rhône (vins-rhone.com) or INAO. No Rayas or Saint Cosme page of the house itself was reached; the importer's technical sheets for Saint Cosme are marked secondary.

A fact in two independent sources or one primary stands; a producer's own claim is hedged as its account; a fact in one secondary only, or nowhere, is softened or taken out and listed here. A writer's own site (Wine with Seth, The Wine Cellar Insider, Vinography, Wine Anorak) and a forum thread were read as leads and never cited, and a Decanter column and interview whose addresses name living people are described here rather than cited. Facts the library states stand as the brief allows, except where a search contested them.

The rules were tried on every string: no living person named, no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, no bare family word, British spelling, no dash; the questions for one right answer, plausible distractors and an explanation that teaches. The lint notes left standing: the first appellations of France (INAO and the appellation's own page), the first of the Villages raised to a cru (Inter Rhône and INAO), and the oldest Mourvèdre, the library's own words for Hommage.

tested: The purchase of 1909 by Pierre Tramier, his son-in-law Pierre Perrin who enlarged the vineyard, and Jacques Perrin, Pierre's son, to his death in 1978 (Wikipedia, the estate's history page, iDealwine, Lea and Sandeman; one account says 1905): confirmed; the author's recollection of a Tramier was right.
The name Beaucastel at Courthézon from 1549, when a Pierre de Beaucastel bought a barn and land at Coudoulet (the estate's history page, Wikipedia): confirmed and dated.

Farming without chemical sprays from the 1950s: the estate's own page credits Jacques Perrin as a forerunner of organic farming from the 1960s and of biodynamics from 1974, and one Wine Spectator profile says 1956; the record follows the estate.
Jacques Perrin bringing back Mourvèdre, a variety that had almost vanished from the appellation (Wine Spectator's Soil Hunters): confirmed.

The blend (the estate's sheets for 2012 and 2019 and a later sheet: Grenache and Mourvèdre about level, Syrah and Counoise next, the rest of the thirteen in small parts): confirmed; the estate grows all thirteen by its own statement.
The site (the estate's own pages: the northern edge of the appellation, exposed to the Mistral, rolled pebbles over sand, clay and limestone): the north east of the draft corrected.

The making (the estate's product page: hand picking, each variety apart, Mourvèdre and Syrah in conical wooden vats; Wine Spectator on the 2010: destemmed, flash heated, two weeks of maceration, cement and steel; the Perrin sheet: total destemming, about fifteen days in vat, then foudres; iDealwine and the Perrin sheet: about a year, twelve months, in large old foudres): confirmed, with the heating now hedged as the estate's long habit; a forum thread citing the estate's former page gives heating to 80 and cooling to 20 degrees Celsius, not carried.
Hommage à Jacques Perrin first made in 1989 by his sons for their father, only in strong years (iDealwine, Decanter's complete vertical from 1989, the estate's Hommage page): confirmed.
Tablas Creek: the Perrins and their American importer bought the Paso Robles land in 1989 by the winery's own history (a Saveur profile of 2004 says 1990): confirmed.
The decree of 1936 among the first appellations of France (INAO, the appellation's own page): confirmed; that the decree itself named the thirteen varieties was found in no source, and is cut.
Jacques Perrin's year of birth: searched once and found nowhere; he stays named with the year of his death only.

The rules: nobody living named (his sons, a later Pierre Perrin of people.json and the importer's son met in results, none carried), no price, no score, nothing volatile, no judging superlative, British, no dash; both questions have one key, options of one kind and an explanation naming the nearest wrong option: sound.

changed.was: Courthézon, on the north eastern edge of Châteauneuf, has known the name Beaucastel since the sixteenth century, when a family of that name held land there. In 1909 the property was bought by an ancestor of the Perrin family, and it has passed down the generations since. Jacques Perrin, who ran it until his death in 1978, set its course: by the family's account he farmed without chemical sprays from the 1950s, and he kept faith with all thirteen of the permitted varieties when many estates grew little but Grenache. Mourvèdre, slow to ripen and hard to grow, became the estate's mark, giving its wine a savoury frame of leather and game, and the brief heating of the harvest before fermentation became its method. When the appellation was founded in 1936 its rules named thirteen grapes, and Beaucastel became the estate that showed what all of them could do together. In 1989 the family first made Hommage à Jacques Perrin, a Mourvèdre led selection kept for strong years, and that same year bought land at Paso Robles with their American importer, the start of Tablas Creek. Mourvèdre belongs in any talk of Châteauneuf because of Beaucastel, the counterweight to Grenache alone.
changed.now: Courthézon, on the northern edge of Châteauneuf, has known the name Beaucastel since 1549, when, by the estate's account, a man of that name bought a barn and land at Coudoulet. In 1909 the property was bought by a forebear of the Perrin family, who rebuilt its vineyard; it passed to his son-in-law, the first Perrin there, who enlarged it, and then to that son-in-law's son, Jacques Perrin, who ran it until his death in 1978. By the estate's account Jacques Perrin was a forerunner of organic farming from the 1960s, and he brought back Mourvèdre, a variety that had almost vanished from the appellation; it gives the wine its savoury frame of leather and game. Châteauneuf-du-Pape, decreed in 1936 among the first appellations of France, allows thirteen varieties, and Beaucastel grows every one of them. In 1989 his sons first made Hommage à Jacques Perrin, a Mourvèdre led selection kept for strong years, and that same year the family and their American importer bought land at Paso Robles in California, the start of Tablas Creek. Mourvèdre belongs in any talk of Châteauneuf because of Beaucastel, the counterweight to Grenache alone.
changed.why: Every beat searched: 1549 and the barn by the estate and Wikipedia; 1909, the son-in-law and Jacques Perrin to 1978 by the estate, Wikipedia and iDealwine; organic farming from the 1960s by the estate; Mourvèdre brought back by Wine Spectator; the decree of 1936 by INAO and the appellation; Hommage by iDealwine and Decanter; Tablas Creek by its own history. The thirteen named in 1936 and the heating tied to Jacques Perrin were found nowhere.

changed.was: Rayas lies in the woods of the north east of Châteauneuf, on sand rather than stone, and the Reynaud family bought it in 1880. In the next generation the estate began to bottle its own wine and to make its name with Grenache alone, though the rules of the appellation, set down in 1936, allowed thirteen varieties. From 1978 the founder's grandson ran it, a reclusive man with little time for visitors, the press or marketing, who kept a dark cellar of old casks and released his wines when he chose. He died in 1997, and his nephew took charge of Rayas and of the family's Château de Fonsalette in the Côtes du Rhône, keeping the same low yields, late picking and old wood. The estate's fame rests on what it showed: that a Châteauneuf could be pale, perfumed and of one grape, and that cool sand could matter as much as the rolled stones for which the appellation is known. Rayas did this with few words and no fashion. Its lesson holds for the cellar and the floor alike: colour and weight are not the measure of a southern red.
changed.now: Rayas lies among woods north east of the village of Châteauneuf, on sand rather than stone. It was founded in 1880 by a notary of the Reynaud family who had lost his hearing and turned to the vine. His son, who had studied agriculture, bottled the estate's first wine in 1920 and printed Premier Grand Cru on its labels, a rank of his own making that exasperated the local authorities, since Châteauneuf has no official classification. He added Château des Tours at Sarrians in the 1930s and Château de Fonsalette in the Côtes du Rhône in 1945. On his death in 1978 one of his sons took charge of Rayas and Fonsalette, until his own sudden death, without children, in 1997. A nephew who had been running Château des Tours then took Rayas on, keeping its Grenache alone, its very low yields and its old wood until his death in 2025. The appellation allows thirteen varieties, yet Rayas showed that a Châteauneuf could be pale, perfumed and of one grape, and that cool sand could matter as much as the rolled stones. Colour and weight, it teaches, are not the measure of a southern red.
changed.why: Every beat searched; the reclusive grandson, his dark cellar and his release dates were found in no source, and the nephew is now known to have died in November 2025.

changed.was: The domaine is named for a tower. Claude Chappe (1763 to 1805) devised the optical telegraph in the 1790s, a chain of towers with movable arms that passed messages across France from hilltop to hilltop, and one of them stood on La Crau, the plateau at the eastern edge of what became Châteauneuf-du-Pape. In 1891, by the family's account, a grower of the Brunier family planted vines on the plateau, among stones so thick that the soil beneath them can barely be seen. The holding grew from generation to generation, and when the appellation was drawn in 1936 the plateau lay within it. The galets roulés, quartzite rounded by the ancient Rhône, store the day's heat and give it back at night, while the red clay beneath holds water through the summer, so the old Grenache ripens fully without drying out. The family kept the old name and made La Crau its flagship, with Télégramme, from younger vines, beside it as a second wine. Ask what the stones of Châteauneuf actually do, and Vieux Télégraphe is the glass that answers.
changed.now: The domaine is named for a tower. In 1891, the year the family dates its work from, the Bruniers began to plant vines on the plateau, among stones so thick that the soil beneath them can barely be seen, and a later generation gave the estate the old tower's name. When the appellation was decreed in 1936 the plateau lay within it. The galets roulés, pebbles carried down from the Alps by the ancient Rhône, store the day's heat and give it back at night, while the clay beneath holds water through the summer, so the old Grenache ripens fully without drying out. The family made La Crau its flagship, with Télégramme, from younger vines, beside it as a second wine. Ask what the stones of Châteauneuf actually do, and Vieux Télégraphe is the glass that answers.

changed.was: Records of the Avril family in Châteauneuf go back, as the family tells it, to the seventeenth century, in a village named for the castle the popes of Avignon built above it in the fourteenth. In 1896, as the family tells it, an Avril bottled wine under the estate name Clos des Papes, when most of the village sold in bulk. In 1923 the growers, led by Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié (1890 to 1967), drew up rules for their wine, on its place, its grapes and its ripeness, that fed into French appellation law, and in 1936 Châteauneuf-du-Pape became an appellation in its own right. Through the twentieth century the family added parcels in every corner of the appellation, until the estate held around two dozen. Where other houses set their old vines apart in prestige cuvées, Clos des Papes kept to one red and one white, and gave the red more Mourvèdre than most, for freshness and structure. That refusal to divide is the estate's signature. On a list it stands for the whole appellation in one bottle, and its white, from six varieties, deserves a place beside it.
changed.now: Records of the Avril family in Châteauneuf go back, as the family tells it, to 1600, in a village named for the castle the popes of Avignon built above it between 1317 and 1333. In 1923 the growers of the village formed a union under Baron Pierre Le Roy de Boiseaumarié (1890 to 1967) to win strict rules on where their wine grew, from which grapes and at what ripeness, and on 15 May 1936 Châteauneuf-du-Pape became one of the first appellations of France. The family's holding grew to around two dozen parcels in every corner of the appellation. Where other houses set their old vines apart in prestige cuvées, Clos des Papes kept to one red and one white, and its red carries more Mourvèdre than most. changed.was: Under the jagged limestone of the Dentelles de Montmirail, Saint Cosme stands on ground worked since Roman times: vats cut into the rock of its cellars are held to be Gallo-Roman, and a chapel of Saint Cosme gave the estate its name. The Barruol family has held it since 1570. For centuries the wine of Gigondas went out without a name of its own, as Côtes du Rhône and later as Côtes du Rhône Villages, until in 1971 the village became the first of the Villages promoted to a cru, red and rosé, with lower yields and a tighter boundary than its neighbours. In the 1990s a new generation of the family took the estate in hand, began to bottle its lieux-dits apart, Valbelle, Le Claux, Hominis Fides and Le Poste, and set up a merchant business beside it for wines from bought grapes. In 2023 the appellation added white wine to its red and rosé. The estate's Gigondas, the blend of its parcels, introduces the house and shows that Gigondas is not simply a Châteauneuf from the next valley.
changed.now: Under the jagged limestone of the Dentelles de Montmirail, Saint Cosme stands on ground worked since Roman times: vats cut into the limestone beneath the château are held to be Gallo-Roman. The Barruol family has been there since 1490 by most accounts, with 1570 in others. Gigondas, long a commune of the Côtes du Rhône Villages, became on 6 January 1971 the first of them raised to a cru of its own, for red and rosé. In 1992 a son of the family took charge after his father fell ill, and later in that decade, by the family's account, set up a merchant business beside the estate for wines from bought grapes, labelled Saint Cosme alone. Beside its Gigondas the estate bottles lieux-dits apart, Le Claux, Hominis Fides and Le Poste, and an old vine Valbelle. From the 2023 vintage the appellation added white wine to its red and rosé. The estate's Gigondas, whole bunches of Grenache with Mourvèdre and Syrah from its own vines, introduces the house and shows that Gigondas is not simply a Châteauneuf from the next valley.
changed.why: The family's 1490 and 1570, the vats, the cru of 6 January 1971, the son of 1992 and the merchant business, Valbelle as a selection; the chapel, the yields and the boundary cut.
